Interview with Jordan Brooks 
of AQR Capital ManagementFrank J. Fabozzi, EditorFrank
 J. Fabozzi: How do you determine the appropriate strategic asset allocation 
for your portfolios? What inputs or assumptions are most critical in anchoring long-term 
allocations?Jordan Brooks: A pair of lessons I came to appreciate more than two decades 
apart informs my thinking about portfolio construction. The rst lesson was from day 
one of freshman economicscasting economic problems in terms of objectives, 
alternatives, and constraints is a very powerful organizational framework. The sec
-
ond lesson came through lived experience working with clients over my professional 
career at AQRinvestors can often make better decisions by simplifying objectives, 
expanding the universe of potential alternatives, and relaxing or eliminating unnec
-
essary and overly binding constraints. These lessons are very general, with applica
-
tions ranging from economic research to human resource management. However, 
they are particularly relevant when considering strategic asset allocation (SAA) in a 
multi-asset portfolio.
Let us start with objectives. In designing a strategic allocation, we begin with the 
premise that investors prefer returns and dislike volatility. If you churn through the 
math, it turns out this statement is equivalent to saying investors seek to maximize 
their risk-adjusted returns or Sharpe ratio.
There are most assuredly things investors care about other than Sharpe ratio 
and the absolute level of returns. Investors tend to be averse to tail risk, for example. 
The average investor will pay more for an asset that tends to hedge equity market 
crashes than for an asset that tends to crash alongside equities. This is why selling 
insurance on the market (via, for example, out-of-the-money equity index puts) pays 
so handsomely. But unless you are meaningfully less averse to tail risk than the 
average investor, I wouldnt advocate writing puts. Balanced performance across dif
-
ferent macroeconomic regimes may also be important to investors, particularly those 
who have liabilities indexed to ination. Tracking error relative to a policy portfolio 
benchmark is yet another consideration that may enter investor objectives. Drawing 
on that career-long learning curve, however, lets start simple: The aim of the SAA is 
to maximize risk
-
adju
sted expected returns.
Next, we move on to the universe of eligible assets. More is generally better. I urge 
investors to embrace geographic and asset class diversication. US stocks and bonds 
are typically included in any SAA. But an SAA that consists of a broader universe of 
global stocks and bonds is likely to have superior long-run returns and more resilient 
performance in protracted bear markets, as noted by Clifford Asness, Roni Israelov, and 
John Liew in their2011 Financial Analyst Journal article, International Diversication 
Works (Eventually). Including commodities, ination-linked bonds, credit, and other 
asset classes in an SAA can further improve long-run performance by helping to but-
tress the SAA through a range of market and macroeconomic environments. In addition 
to diversication, the other major consideration is liquidity. Investors build a strategic 
asset allocation to generate returns to fund current or future liabilities, whether pension 
obligations or personal retirement aspirations. Investors must design an SAA that can 
provide liquidity when needed. Ideally, an SAA with sufcient exposure to highly liquid 
instruments will provide investors with ample choices of where to tap liquidity and 
adjust exposures based on respective opportunity sets and the market environment.
Jordan Brooksis co-head of macro 
strategies at AQR 
Capital Management in 
Greenwich, CT.
jordan.brooks@aqr.com

Interview with Jordan Brooks of AQR Capital Management
Multi-Asset Special Issue 2026That brings us to constraints. Here less is typically more. Many investors, for 
example, constrain themselves to hold an unlevered portfolio. Forcing a portfolio to 
be precisely100% invested may lead to more return-seeking investors overinvesting 
in stocks. Removing this constraint and permitting leverage allows investors to hold 
the optimal (i.e., Sharpe ratiomaximizing) mix of stocks, bonds, and other assets, 
and to lever this tangency portfolio up or down based on desired risk tolerance or 
to achieve their desired return target.
What does all this add up to? We aim to build a liquid SAA with attractive 
risk-adjusted returns by investing globally across asset classes. The remaining 
inputs in this stylized example are expected risk-adjusted returns of different asset 
classes and expected correlations across asset classes. To estimate these inputs, 
we dig into the data. We use estimates of unconditional expected returns in SAA 
construction (time-varying expected returns, whether slower-moving valuation-based or 
higher-frequency momentum-based, are potential inputs in tactical asset allocation). 
While over decade-long periods any one asset class may signicantly outperform, 
over longer samples risk-adjusted returns of different asset classes (e.g.,stocks, 
bonds, commodities) are similar. The last 10 years have been great for US stocks. 
20002009, not so much, but it was a great period for bonds. Longer-term data also 
shows that different asset classes have averaged low correlations to one another. 
Asset class Sharpe ratios that are more similar than different, coupled with low 
correlations across asset classes, imply the optimal SAA should have a good chunk 
of risk coming from different asset classes.
This simple exercise produces an SAA that is meaningfully different from most 
traditional asset allocations. A typical policy benchmark for institutional and retail 
investors is something like a60% stocks plus40% bonds (60/40) portfolio. Because 
stocks are much more volatile than bonds, this policy portfolio is dominated by equity 
risk. In contrast, the optimal SAA will be much more risk-balanced. You can play with 
expected-return assumptions and layer in some of the other considerations I outlined 
above. However, you will still end up with something that is much more risk-balanced 
(and actually diversied) than a60/40 portfolio.Fabozzi: What role does tactical asset allocation play relative to strategic 
allocation? How frequently do tactical decisions materially alter portfolio outcomes?Brooks: Tactical asset allocation (TAA), thoughtfully implemented and appro
-
priately sized, can be very complementary to an SAA. If a key input in SAA is 
long-term, unconditional expected returns across asset classes, the key input in 
TAA is shorter-term, conditional expected returns for each individual asset in the SAA 
(and potentially assets outside the SAA).
A powerful and transparent approach to TAA is trend following. Trend-following 
strategies go long recent winners and short recent losers. Because asset prices tend 
to underreact to new information, a strategy going long markets with rising prices 
(good news) and short markets with falling prices (bad news) tends to be protable 
on average. Trend-following strategies can be very complementary to SAAs for two 
reasons. First, since trend programs take both long and short positions (typically with 
close to equal frequency), they are very lowly correlated to an SAA. Second, because 
the largest equity market drawdowns have tended to be persistentthink the tech 
bust, global nancial crisis (GFC), and ination surge of2022trend following has 
historically performed exceptionally well when equities have done poorly. In industry 
parlance, trend following is convex to equities. Thats a nice feature.
Trend-following strategies have generally delivered. Since2000, the SocGen 
Trend index (SG Trend), an equal-weighted average of the 10 largest trend-following 
managers, has delivered returns roughly on par with a global60/40 portfolio and 
has performed exceptionally well during the three largest equity market drawdowns.

Multi-Asset Special Issue 2026Typically, one needs to pay for insurance-like characteristics. Trend following has pro
-
vided exceptional diversication precisely when investors have needed it most and 
has realized positive average returns. You dont need to look far back to see that trend 
following materially improves portfolio outcomes. In2022, a global60/40 portfolio 
returned 

15%; the SG Trend index returned27%.
An oft-cited complaint about trend following is performance may languish for long 
periods between drawdowns. While the SG Trend index returned27% in2022, its 
been effectively at from January2023 through December2025. My advice here is 
two-fold. First, be patient! Middling performance in good times is a price worth paying 
for an investment that pays off handsomely when you need it most. Second, this is 
where manager selection comes into play. At AQR, trend following has been one of our 
most innovative research areas over the past several years. Unfortunately, I cant go 
too deep into details here in writing. But we utilize a much more sophisticated model 
incorporating measures of fundamental trends in addition to price trends (which can 
be particularly helpful in navigating turning points and whipsawing markets), and we 
trade a vast and highly unique investment universe. These innovations have helped 
us deliver on the dual mandate of trend following: strong average performance and 
exceptional performance in bear-market environments.
Trend following is not the only game in town when it comes to TAA, but it is 
among the lowest-hanging fruit. It is easier to underwrite than many other strategies, 
and its convexity to equities makes it particularly appealing. But a more elaborate 
TAA program that takes relative value views across markets within an asset class 
(e.g.,overweight US Treasuries and underweight German Bunds) or across different 
stocks within an index, based on myriad inputs including but not limited to price and 
fundamental trends, relative valuations, investor sentiment extracted via alternative 
data, etc., can complement both an SAA and trend program.Fabozzi: How do macroeconomic conditions and regime shifts enter your 
allocation process? Are regimes modeled explicitly, or reected through scenarios 
and judgment?Brooks: Again, I think it is helpful to start with the basics. In our SAA, we aim to 
maximize risk-adjusted returns. A key input in portfolio construction is asset class 
correlations. But asset class correlations are deeply dependent on macroeconomic 
regimes. For example, in a research article that I coauthored with my AQR colleagues 
(Ale Brixton, Pete Hecht, Antti Ilmanen, Thomas Maloney, and Nicholas McQuinn), 
published in the2023 JPM special issue on multi-asset strategies (A Changing 
StockBond Correlation: Drivers and Implications), we discussed that low-frequency 
variation in the stockbond correlation tends to be driven by the relative volatility 
of growth versus ination shocks. When growth tends to be more variable (think 
late1990s through2020), bonds and stocks tend to be negatively correlated. When 
ination tends to be more variable (think1970s through1980s, and again more 
recently), bonds and stocks tend to be positively correlated.
Suppose your SAA is risk-balanced across equities and nominal bonds. If you are 
sitting in late2020 or early2021 and you are estimating asset class correlations 
using some trailing window, your SAA looks highly diversied. Stocks and bonds have 
been negatively correlated with one another, and you expect that if the stock market 
is down your bond allocation will offset some of the losses. But then you get a big 
ination shock, and stocks and bonds drawdown together. You were sitting on a lot 
more risk than you thought.
If you could predict correlations with certainty, this wouldnt concern you. If you 
knew the stockbond correlation was going to be higher over the next year, youd 
hold less of each, and more of other diversifying assets. But it is challenging to 
predict correlations with a high degree of accuracy because correlations depend on

Interview with Jordan Brooks of AQR Capital Management
Multi-Asset Special Issue 2026macroeconomic shocks that are themselves hard to forecast. Accordingly, we take 
a much humbler approach. We design our strategic allocation so that performance 
is somewhat balanced across different macroeconomic regimes. Continuing with 
the example above, a risk-balanced stock-and-bond portfolio has a highly negative 
sensitivity to an ination shock. Adding commodities or replacing some nominal 
bonds with ination-linked bonds reins in this negative ination exposure. You can 
do a similar exercise for growth and monetary policy (interest rate) sensitivity; we 
do so.
Simply stated, we dont attempt to forecast macroeconomic regime changes. 
Counting on any investor to do that reliably is a fools errand. But we try to build an 
SAA that is robust
 to changing regimes.
In our trend-followingbased TAA strategies, we explicitly aim to prot from mac
-
roeconomic shocks and regime changes. Asset prices underreact to new information, 
so we go long markets with favorable macroeconomic shocks and short markets with 
adverse macroeconomic shocks, betting that shocks will have a persistent impact 
on prices. Indeed, we observe that performance tends to be better when macroeco
-
nomic volatility is higher.Fabozzi: How do you incorporate ination risk across a multi-asset portfolio? Which 
assets or strategies have proven most effective in addressing ination uncertainty?Brooks: Ination is one of the primary macroeconomic risk factors we would like 
to have minimal sensitivity to. That is easier said than done, since both stocks and 
bonds tend to be negatively exposed to ination shocks. A multi-asset-class SAA is, 
therefore, likely to trade short ination. The question is how short, and what can be 
done in SAA and TAA programs to mitigate ination risk?
Measuring the ination sensitivity of different asset classes is nontrivial. Consis
-
tent with academic literature (a good recent reference is the2025 Review of Financial 
Studies
 article by Xiang Fang, Yang Liu, and Nikolai Roussanov, Getting to the Core: 
Ination Risks Within and Across Asset Classes), we nd it is important to separate 
ination into two components: core ination and food and energy ination (which 
together sum to headline ination). It turns out asset classes may have quite different 
sensitivities to core and food/energy ination shocks. Nominal bonds are negatively 
exposed to both. Equities are negatively exposed to core ination but hold up well in 
food/energy ination. Commodities are often considered an inationary hedge, but 
a caveat applies. Historically theyve been an excellent hedge against food/energy 
ination but not core ination.
Consider an SAA that is roughly risk-balanced between stocks, nominal bonds, 
and commodities. The food/energy ination sensitivity of the SAA should be small: 
Bonds will do poorly in an ination spike, but commodities will do well. The portfolio 
is negatively exposed to core ination, however. In a core ination shock, stocks and 
bonds sell off, and commodities dont help. Among liquid asset classes, ination 
breakevens (long an ination-linked bond, short a nominal bond with equal duration) 
are unique in their ability to hedge core ination shocks. To reduce the SAAs sensi
-
tivity to core ination, we therefore add ination breakevens. Since we are starting 
with an allocation that contains nominal bonds, this amounts to substituting some 
nominal bond exposure with ination-linked bonds.
A trend-followingbased TAA program may also provide diversication against 
ination risk. Generally, trend following strategies perform well when there are 
substantial shocks to economic fundamentals, as such changes tend to produce 
large asset price adjustmentstypically across multiple asset classes. Often, these 
price adjustments are gradual and persistent as market participants underreact to 
new fundamental realities, reecting one of the core inefciencies trend followers aim 
to exploit. In other words, trend following tends to nd some of its best opportunities

Multi-Asset Special Issue 2026during periods of macroeconomic shocks and fundamental volatility. An inationary 
environment is one specic example of this, and we do, in fact, see trend-following 
strategies perform very well during such episodes. In their2017 JPM paper, 
 
A Century of Trend Following, Brian Hurst, Yao Hua Ooi, and Lasse Pedersen found 
the best decade (returns and Sharpe ratio) for trend following was the1970s, a period 
of strongly rising commodity prices, ination, and interest rates (alongside major 
recessions). More recently, the rapid rise in core ination that took place in2022 
was the best year for the SG Trend index in its history (since2000). Overall, we nd 
trend following can be a key input in building a portfolio that can successfully navigate 
core and headline inationary environments.Fabozzi: What role do alternatives play within your multi-asset framework? 
 
How do you balance their potential diversication benets against liquidity and 
valuation concerns?Brooks: Not all alternatives are created equalwith respect to their diversication 
properties, their liquidity, and their transparency. We tend to focus on liquid, publicly 
traded instruments to create exposures that are truly diversifying to traditional 
investments like stocks and bonds.
Commodity futures are a canonical example and serve an essential role in our 
SAA. They are liquid, have historically paid a positive risk premium, and are diversi
-
fying relative to stocks and bonds, particularly during inationary episodes. Diversi
-
ed corporate credit spread exposure is another example. While credit spreads and 
equities are positively correlated, they are not perfectly correlated. And credit risk 
tends to outperform equities (beta-adjusted) in rising interest rate environments. 
Including commodities and credit spread exposure in an SAA can help provide better 
macroeconomic balance and superior long-term risk-adjusted returns.
Longshort liquid alternatives (i.e.,trend-following, market-neutral stock 
selection, and relative value global asset allocation) can be very additive on top of a 
multi-asset-class SAA. They tend to be lowly correlated to traditional asset classes, 
and portfolios that include them can potentially realize better risk-adjusted returns 
and more balanced performance across macroeconomic regimes. Given the current 
backdrop of exceptionally rich equity market valuations and market concentration, 
longshort liquid alternatives are arguably even more important in a portfolio than 
they have been historically.
Many popular alternatives, however, are not that alternative. Private equity (PE), 
for example, is subject to the same return driversthe ability of rms to grow cash 
ows and the valuations investors put on those cash owsas public equities. A bad 
decade for the stock market will be a bad decade for PE. Its lack of mark-to-market 
might make it seem like a diversier, but that diversication is largely ephemeral. Does 
this imply PE has no place in an SAA? Not necessarily, at least for investors who are 
comfortable with the illiquidity (which may be a feature not a bug and, therefore, drive 
down long-term expected returns, as Cliff Asness discusses in a short2019 note, 
The Illiquidity Discount), assuming they account for its correlation to public equities.Fabozzi: How do you integrate quantitative models with qualitative judgment? 
 
In which areas do models dominate, and where does discretion remain essential?Brooks: AQR stands for Applied Quantitative Researchwe are a quant rm. 
This means we follow our models: Our positions and trades are determined by heav
-
ily researched and backtested algorithms. This does not mean, however, that our 
investment process is devoid of discretion. Our discretion manifests in the design 
of the models. For SAA, what are our objectives, alternatives, and constraints? How 
much do we weigh having the best empirical Sharpe ratio based on historical cor
-
relations against having balanced performance across macroeconomic regimes?

Interview with Jordan Brooks of AQR Capital Management
Multi-Asset Special Issue 2026What methodologies do we use to estimate asset class expected returns? For TAA, 
what are the different signals determining whether we are long or short each asset 
(and with what size)? Our debates sitting around the table are not about whether to 
be long or short crude, rather they are about the inputs to the models that determine 
our ultimate view on crude.
Quants exercising discretion in the design of their models is true for any systematic 
rm, but it is especially true at AQR where the majority of the quantitative signals 
we employ relate back to fundamentally driven market inefciencies. We identify 
persistent and pervasive phenomena, like the tendency of asset prices to underreact 
to new information. Then we build numerous quantitative signals using myriad data 
sources (traditional, alternative, and proprietary) to capitalize on underreaction. 
 
We are continuously looking to identify new market inefciencies, build new signals 
to capitalize on these market inefciencies, and add new assets to our investable 
universe. We are quantitative in implementation, but qualitative judgment is crucial 
in the research process.Fabozzi: How has the availability of new data and AI-driven tools inuenced asset 
allocation decisions? Where have these tools added the most value, and where have 
expectations fallen short?Brooks: In SAA, the impact of new data and ML/AI-driven tools is modest. As weve 
discussed, the primary inputs in SAA are estimates of long-run expected risk-adjusted 
returns, correlations, and macroeconomic sensitivities. Alternative datasets and 
natural language processing do not directly address these inputs.
In TAA, however, new data and tools have already added signicant value. 
 
In our investment approach, there are three potential avenues for novel data, ML, and 
 
AI to add value: (1) identifying new market inefciencies, (2) improving our ability 
to capitalize on previously identied market inefciencies through new signals, and 
 
(3) better portfolio construction.
I think (1) is what people typically think of when they hear about big data and 
ML/AI at investment rms. You throw a whole bunch of data into a fancy estimation 
algorithm, and it solves the market and spits out protable positions. Maybe there is 
some scope for this in the high-frequency world of statistical arbitrage, but less so in 
our investment strategies trading liquid markets with holding periods that range from 
weeks to months. Samples are too short, and markets are too efcient. (Ronen Israel, 
Bryan Kelly, and Tobias Moskowitz discuss these challenges in detail in their2019 
Journal of Investment Management article, Can Machines Learn Finance?) (2) and 
(3) are where we have found a lot of value in TAA (and especially in more data-rich 
stock selection). New data sets and AI tools like natural language processing have 
led to the development of new and complementary signals. And in an asset and 
signalrich environment, ML-based estimation techniques have led to improvements 
in strategic and tactical signal weighting. Here, again, I need to play it close to the 
vest. But sufce it to say I think the marriage of a fundamentally driven investment 
process where we aim to capitalize on a set of identiable market inefciencies and 
new data and ML/AI-driven tools is a very powerful union.Fabozzi: How do you evaluate success in a multi-asset strategy? Beyond returns, 
what performance dimensions are most informative?Brooks: OK, I need to start with returnsthey are what we eat at the end of 
the day. We design our multi-asset-class portfolios with the explicit objective of 
maximizing risk-adjusted returns. Examining historical long-run performance of dif
-
ferent asset classes, as well as their pairwise correlations, a risk-balanced SAA can 
hopefully achieve a0.5 Sharpe ratio over the long runcash plus5%, assuming 
the SAA targets10% volatility. How have risk-balanced SAAs performed in practice?

Multi-Asset Special Issue 2026Since the inception of the HFR Risk Parity index in2003, its historical Sharpe ratio 
is0.55. Absolute performance has been as advertised.
But stand-alone absolute performance isnt the nal word. Too often investors 
make a direct comparison between multi-asset SAA and more traditional portfolios, 
such as60/40 or all equities. They ask which portfolio has greater returns or the 
better Sharpe ratio. But this is relevant only when an investors choice set is limited 
to investing all their money in one portfolio or the other. Portfolio choice, however, is 
not binary! The relevant question is whether a multi-asset-class strategy is additive 
on top of an investors existing portfolio, which is typically very heavily invested in 
equities. When determining whether (and how much) to invest in a multi-asset-class 
portfolio relative to a traditional all stock or60/40 portfolio, the stand-alone Sharpe 
ratio of the multi-asset-class portfolio matters, but so does its correlation. The key 
empirical question is whether the multi-asset SAA has alpha relative to traditional 
portfolios (i.e.,is it complementary)? This is a lower bar, but the more important 
one to clear. Viewed through this lens, the empirical case for including risk-balanced 
multi-asset strategies within strategic allocations is strengthened, which Cliff Asness 
discusses in detail in his2015 note, Risk Parity Is Even Better than We Thought.
Additionally, and perhaps most critically, when you consider the ultimate purpose 
of an SAA (i.e.,to grow and protect capital to meet some future obligations), 
 
a risk-balanced SAA should provide more resilient performance through a range of 
market and macroeconomic environments. Further, a risk-balanced SAA tends to have 
more muted drawdowns than a more concentrated portfolio like the traditional60/40, 
which is almost entirely beholden to the fate of equity markets. While modest under
-
performance of a risk-balanced SAA during bull markets can be frustrating, a multiyear 
capital loss from a large equity drawdown (e.g.,the GFC or tech bust) in a traditional 
portfolio can be catastrophic. The risk-balanced SAAs combination of an attractive 
absolute return that tends to be more robust across macroeconomic and market 
regimes, along with more muted drawdowns and highly liquid holdings, should help 
set up an investor for better long-term success.Fabozzi: How do you think about tail risk in a multi-asset context? What approaches 
have you found most effective in managing extreme but plausible outcomes?Brooks: Tail risk in a multi-asset context typically arises from one of two sources. 
The rst is when an individual market or asset class experiences a large, discrete, 
adverse event and sells off. The second is death by a thousand cuts, where assets 
that had appeared to diversify one another become highly correlated and underperform 
together.
To address the rst source, we must move beyond volatility as the sole risk 
metric used for sizing positions. Volatility, or standard deviation, measures dispersion 
around the mean and treats positive and negative outcomes symmetrically. But not all 
volatility is created equal. This is where blending SAA and TAA kicks in. By pairing an 
SAA with a convex TAA program, such as trend following, you can distinguish between 
bad volatility (e.g.,nominal bonds in2022) and good volatility (e.g.,equity markets 
in2025), reducing downside participation while preserving upside participation.
The second source is admittedly more challenging. Asset correlations are highly 
uid, and rare or novel events can prompt co-movements that have not been observed 
previously. This is where you need humility. As I talked about before, you cant reliably 
forecast large changes in correlations, as they are dependent on macroeconomic 
news. However, a robust portfolio design and investment process can help you reduce 
portfolio sensitivity to correlation misestimation. In practice, this means estimating 
correlations over long horizons to avoid overreliance on unstable cross-asset rela
-
tionships and imposing prudent leverage limits so that sudden correlation spikes do 
not translate into outsize losses.

Interview with Jordan Brooks of AQR Capital Management
Multi-Asset Special Issue 2026Fabozzi: How do you think about diversication when correlations rise during 
periods of stress? Which forms of diversication remain most reliable in such 
environments?Brooks: I have spilled a good amount of ink stressing the importance of geographic 
and asset class diversication. But one dimension of diversication I have so far 
neglected to discuss is time series diversication. In times of rising correlations 
and market stress, the volatility of an SAA is likely to increase. However, unless the 
forward-looking expected Sharpe ratio of the SAA rises in lockstep (and there is little 
reason to think it typically should), investor risk tolerance probably has not.
If you maintain constant exposure, you may be forced to sell parts of your portfolio 
at a bad time (a fate many investors endured during the GFC). I think this point is 
generally appreciated and motivates various drawdown control mechanisms. A less 
appreciated point, however, is that a portfolio with time-varying risks, even if you 
can hold it over the long term, isnt optimal either. Time-varying volatility reduces 
risk-adjusted returns, so your long-term returns will come disproportionately from 
stressful environments. A prudent SAA will aim to target a relatively constant level 
of volatility over time. The benets arent just that such a portfolio is easier to hold 
in stress environments, but that long-term returns arent driven by the handful of 
periods when market volatility was high.
Of course, volatility and correlation forecasting models arent perfect. They might 
be easier to get right than returns, but you still want humility and guardrails. Having 
prudent limits on asset class and overall leverage embedded in the portfolio construc
-
tion process can be helpful constraints to further enforce diversication through time.
Finally, a trend-followingbased TAA program may help navigate periods of market 
stress and rising correlations as well. Typically, prolonged periods of market stress 
and shifts in correlation have a fundamental catalyst (e.g.,rising ination or a hawkish 
shift in monetary policy). If the impact on markets unfolds gradually, trend-based TAA 
programs will tend to reduce exposures to affected assets until the bearish catalyst 
wears off. This is yet another reason a trend-following TAA program can be a powerful 
addition to an SAA.
